title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind

contents: Part One, The Cognitive Revolution: how a middling ape began cooperating in large numbers through shared fictions (~70,000 years ago)
Part Two, The Agricultural Revolution: farming as 'history's biggest fraud' — more food, worse lives, and no way back (~10,000 BCE)
Part Three, The Unification of Humankind: money, empire, and universal religions as the great convergers
Part Four, The Scientific Revolution: the discovery of ignorance, the marriage of science, empire, and capital, and the question of happiness (~1500 CE onward)

audiences: General readers wanting one grand narrative of the species
Book clubs and students entering the humanities
Anyone puzzling over money, nations, and religion as institutions

sources.title: Sapiens
sources.supports: The US Harper hardcover's publication date, ISBN and 464-page count; a positive review of the book's concise, vigorous handling of major debates and competing views.

sources.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
sources.supports: US edition metadata, the three named revolutions, the fictive-language thesis, the happiness question, and a balanced verdict: provocative and entertaining but limited to skimming the surface.
sources.limitations: Short trade review; it does not test the book field by field.

sources.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind by Yuval Noah Harari – review
sources.supports: The book's main historical arc, engaging delivery, agriculture and happiness arguments, and specific criticism of careless causal claims, exaggeration and sensationalism.
sources.limitations: A philosopher's newspaper review, not a systematic review of every discipline covered.

sources.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind review – thrilling story, dark message
sources.supports: The four-part structure and a balanced assessment: clear, witty, erudite and thrilling, but broad-brush, occasionally over-simple and prone to overstating science's role in colonialism.
sources.limitations: Professional review rather than peer-reviewed scholarship.

sources.title: A Response to Yuval Harari's Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
sources.author_or_publisher: C. R. Hallpike, New English Review
sources.supports: A career anthropologist's documented assessment: the summaries of accepted knowledge are serviceable, but 'whenever he tries to strike out on his own he often gets things wrong' — the book is not 'a serious contribution to knowledge'.
sources.limitations: A strongly polemical essay in an ideological magazine, not peer review; useful as one named anthropologist's critique, not as field consensus.

sources.title: The Dangerous Populist Science of Yuval Noah Harari
sources.supports: An evolutionary biologist's documented error catalogue: animal 'vocal languages' misstated, chimpanzees fighting cheetahs they never geographically meet, the Waorani miscast as evidence for state pacification — plus the 'science populist' charge and the thesis-advisor quote about asking questions too large to be wrong.
sources.limitations: An expert-authored essay in an advocacy magazine, not peer review; its examples are specific but its wider verdict remains the author's.

sources.title: The revolution that wasn't: a new interpretation of the origin of modern human behavior
sources.author_or_publisher: Sally McBrearty and Alison S. Brooks, Journal of Human Evolution
sources.supports: Primary specialist counterevidence to a sudden late Cognitive Revolution: modern human behaviour accumulated in Africa over a long period rather than appearing as a single abrupt package.
sources.limitations: Published before Sapiens and therefore evaluates the underlying archaeological model, not Harari's book.

sources.title: The Agricultural Revolution as Environmental Catastrophe: Implications for Health and Lifestyle in the Holocene
sources.author_or_publisher: Clark Spencer Larsen, Annual Review of Anthropology
sources.supports: Bioarchaeological evidence that the shift to agriculture often reduced health and quality of life, while also enabling population growth and complex societies.
sources.limitations: Supports an important part of Harari's agriculture argument, not his complete 'fraud' framing or every society.

sources.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
sources.supports: The author's own framing of the book's questions and its origin in his Hebrew University world-history course.
sources.limitations: Author-controlled promotional framing; authoritative for the book's intended claims, not for whether they are correct.

sources.title: Yuval Noah Harari, prophète contesté de la big history
sources.supports: A retrospective account of Harari's place in big history, his narrative method and influence, plus named scholarly objections to controversial interpretation and overbroad generalisation.
sources.limitations: A journalistic profile in French; it surveys rather than independently adjudicates every disputed claim.

sources.title: Prof. Yuval Noah Harari
sources.author_or_publisher: Hebrew University of Jerusalem, History Department
sources.supports: Harari's Oxford PhD, original specialisms in world, medieval and military history, current macrohistorical research questions and main books.
sources.limitations: Official employer profile; authoritative for credentials and research topics, not an independent evaluation of his work.

workflow.coverage_notes: Checked against publisher and national-library records, the author's stated thesis, four direct professional reviews or profiles, two expert critical essays, and peer-reviewed archaeology and bioarchaeology used to test major claims. No full text was supplied, so coverage remains sample-and-secondary.
